# Design, development and evaluation of a human-computer trust scale

Siddharth Gulati, Sonia Sousa and David Lamas

School of Digital Technologies, Tallinn University, Tallinn, Estonia

## ABSTRACT

New technologies, data, and algorithms impact nearly every aspect of daily life. Unfortunately, many of these algorithms operate like black boxes and cannot explain their results even to their programmers, let alone to end-users. As more and more tasks get delegated to such intelligent systems and the nature of user interactions with them becomes increasingly complex, it is important to understand the amount of trust that a user is willing to place on such systems. However, attempts at quantifying trust have either been limited in their scope or not empirically thorough. To address this, we build on prior work which empirically modelled trust in usertechnology interactions and describe the development and evolution of a human computer trust scale. We present results of two studies (N=118 & N=183) which were undertaken to assess the reliability and validity of the proposed scale. Our study contributes to the literature by (a) developing a multi-dimensional scale to assess user trust in HCI and (b) being the first study to use the concept of design fiction and future scenarios to study trust.

instrument development;

## 1. Introduction

**Trust has been a topic which has been receiving increased attention within the human computer interaction (HCI) community, as is evident from some recent publications (Sousa, Lamas, and Dias 2014; Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018; Lewis, Sycara, and Walker 2018; Yagoda and Gillan 2012). Much of this increased interest can be attributed to developments in the** fi**eld of arti**fi**cial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (Kuipers 2018). For instance, developments in AI have allowed concepts such as driverless cars, autonomous drone delivery systems, collaborative robots as teammates, robotic concierges/hosts, etc. which were once thought of as science** fi**ction to not just be brought to reality but also used by many across the globe on a daily basis (Dalcher 2016; Lewis, Sycara, and Walker 2018). Intelligent algorithms are slowly becoming the norm in the present society. As they encroach more into our daily lives, they are making decisions that directly** eff**ect individuals and society as a whole. Unfortunately, many of these algorithms cannot explain their results even to their programmers, let alone to end-users. As we will explain in the next section, there have been instances of such technologies making incorrect and even life-threatening decisions which have had unintended and disastrous consequences. Therefore, in such situations, as the user becomes more vulnerable and uncertain as to how the system might respond, it** **becomes imperative for technologists and researchers alike to understand how much trust does an end user actually place on the advice or recommendations provided to them by such intelligent systems. There are several reasons which make the pursuit of understanding and measuring trust important. Some of these include:**

. **It helps in reducing risk, uncertainty and anxiety associated with a technological interaction (Söllner et al. 2012).**

. **It helps create positive and meaningful experiences with technology (Mcknight et al. 2011).**

. **Is crucial in helping a user adopt and maintain a gradual and steady relationship with the system (Benbasat and Wang 2005).**

**Keeping in mind that trust e**ff**ects so many facets of a user interaction with technology, measuring it is a useful endeavor. Yet despite its importance, prior research on understanding and measuring trust has mainly focused on technology-mediated interactions and relatively less attention has been paid on measuring it in user technology interactions (Mcknight et al. 2011; Söllner et al. 2012; Benbasat and Wang 2005; Vance, Elie-Dit-Cosaque, and Straub 2008). Although, there have been some recent attempts (Sousa, Lamas, and Dias 2014; Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018) to move towards development of a psychometric instrument to measure trust in user** **technology interactions, but the authors of these works further stress the need to test their model in di**ff**erent contexts to ascertain if the trust attributes proposed in their model hold true and would allow to move towards scale development. Through the present study, we build on these prior works and empirically assesses their suitability in user technology interactions. We also explain why these works were speci**fi**cally chosen and in doing so, we describe the development and evolution of a human computer trust scale.**

## 2. Background

**Up until now, the dominant paradigm of user interaction with technology had been the screen. But technological advancements have paved the way for more complex and multi-modal forms of interaction. For instance, tangible, physical, audio and aural modes of user interaction with technical artifacts are becoming more pervasive (Van Hove et al. 2018). Not only is the size of the screen getting smaller, but the underlying technology driving screen-based interactions is getting larger and complex. The development of intelligent algorithms, made possible due to advancements in AI and machine learning are driving most of our day-to-day interactions with digital technology (Hengstler, Enkel, and Duelli 2016; Andras et al. 2018). From a simple google search to product and movie recommendations on Amazon and Net**fl**ix to more complex tasks such as being able to manage an electric power grid or helping doctors make crucial decisions when diagnosing patients, intelligent algorithms are encroaching more into our day to day lives and have the capacity to reason and make decisions on behalf of their human counterparts (Holmquist 2017; Kuipers 2018).**

**Given the unrelenting pace of technological progress, this trend of delegating more responsibilities to machine and the latter becoming increasingly intelligent is not likely to slow down as the continued economic growth is set to depend on it (Hengstler, Enkel, and Duelli 2016). However, despite these technological advances, there have been several instances when use of such technologies have had unintended and disastrous consequences. For instance, IBM recently pitched its Watson supercomputer as ‘Watson for Oncology’**<strong><sup>1</sup></strong>**and put forth that the AI embedded supercomputer would bring about a revolution in cancer treatment and will help doctors make informed decisions based on the recommendations it provides. However, since its rollout, not only are the recommendations provided by Watson not trusted by the doctors, but some have also complained that these recommendations are biased towards American patients and methods of care. Furthermore,** **the actual capabilities of Watson are not well understood by the physicians and hospitals where it has been put to use (Schmidt 2017). On similar lines, there have been concerns raised by medical professionals on relying on AI for making sensitive decisions related to an individual’s health (Maddox, Rumsfeld, and Payne 2019). If the amount of trust that physicians have in such technology is low, then this also has a cascade e**ff**ect on the patients who would also not trust the diagnosis which is o**ff**ered by such modern intelligent systems. There have been other instances as well wherein use of AI infused systems has been disruptive, confusing, o**ff**ensive and even dangerous. Some of these are:**

. **A Google algorithm used in Google Photos, which uses sophisticated AI to perform facial recognition mistakenly classi**fi**ed people of color as gorillas, a move which drew widespread criticism and outrage (Pachal 2019).**

. **An AI enabled self-driving Uber ran a red light in San Francisco, which once again prompted questions among government authorities after the Tesla car crash**<strong><sup>2</sup></strong>**if autonomous vehicles can be trusted to maintain civilian safety (Davies 2019).**

. **Another instance where use of AI enabled technologies sparked mistrust was when the facial-recognition algorithm of Massachusetts registry of motor vehicles mistakenly tagged someone as criminal and revoked their driver’s license (Dormehl 2019).**

**These are some, among the growing examples where use of AI systems has had unintended consequences. Consequently, the amount of trust which the public has on technical artefacts embedded with AI is also low. This is consistent with the result of scienti**fic fi**ndings (Hengstler, Enkel, and Duelli 2016) and public surveys (PEGA 2019), both of which have found that the likelihood of individuals placing trust on the advice and recommendations o**ff**ered by such systems is low. There are several reasons which create uncertainty and lack of trust associated with an AI system. First, the class of machine learning algorithms which are behind the progress of the AI systems (collectively referred to as deep learning algorithms) are opaque, di**ffi**cult to understand and produce a combination of inputs and outputs so large that an everyday AI practitioner is faced with an enormous challenge to** fi**nd the right algorithm which might suit the objective at hand (Holmquist 2017). Second, even if an algorithm is identi**fi**ed, many of these algorithms cannot explain their results even to their programmers, let alone to end-users. They operate like black boxes (i.e. devices that can be viewed in terms of their inputs and outputs, without any knowledge of** **their internal workings) and cannot explain how they arrived to their decisions (Andras et al. 2018; Mols 2019). These factors, coupled with the fact that AI is percolating through modern society and more responsibilities are being abrogated to such intelligent systems in di**ff**erent spheres of life at an unprecedented pace, it is important that trust-related issues with such technologies be systematically studied (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2018; Dalcher 2016; Kuipers 2018). However, as pointed out earlier, prior research has mainly focused on studying trust in technology-mediated interactions and research on studying trust with technical artefacts is still in its infancy. Moreover, the attempts which have been made to quantify trust with such artefacts have either been limited in their scope or not empirically thorough (Söllner et al. 2012; Vance, Elie-Dit-Cosaque, and Straub 2008; Mcknight et al. 2011). Through this research, we build on prior works (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018) to abridge this gap and develop a psychometric instrument to assess user trust with technology. Before doing so, we discuss some past attempts to measure trust in the next section.**

## 2.1. Past attempts to measure trust

**One of the earliest attempts to measure trust in technology was that of Muir and Moray (1996) who measured machine operators trust in the context of industrial automation. While novel at that time, the technological landscape has changed immensely since then and the scale has not been revised to ascertain if it would still be able to measure trust. Following that, Madsen and Gregor (2000) proposed a human computer trust scale. However, the validity of the scale is questionable because of its low sample size and no full empirical validation of the scale has been reported till date (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017; Lewis, Sycara, and Walker 2018). In the same year, another attempt at measuring trust was reported by Jian, Bisantz, and Drury (2000). Their attempt was systematic, thorough and novel but lacked empirical validation. As a result, the scale was not used until recently when an attempt to validate it was carried out by Spain, Bustamante, and Bliss (2008). However, similar to Madsen and Gregor (2000), the sample size for their validation study was low (a limitation which the authors themselves acknowledge) and since then, no studies have been carried out to validate this scale further.**

**Moving on, a shape automation trust index (SATI) scale was developed by the European organisation for the safety of air navigation (Goillau et al. 2019). Even though the individual attributes in their scale have reliabilities in the high 80’s, the overall instrument has** **not been empirically validated since its inception (Lewis, Sycara, and Walker 2018). A more recent attempt at measuring trust is that of Yagoda and Gillan (2012) who propose a scale to measure trust in human robot interaction. However, one of the main drawbacks with this scale is that it cannot be solely administered on its own and has to be coupled with Rotter’s interpersonal trust inventory (Rotter 1967). This not only makes administration of the scale cumbersome but also makes it di**ffi**cult to comprehend (Lewis, Sycara, and Walker 2018). Finally, Rieser and Bernhard (2016) proposed a semantic di**ff**erential scale to measure trust. However, validation of a semantic di**ff**erential scale is a complex process which has not been reported in their work. There are two main limitations with their work which are: (1) they have not tested the relevance of the bipolar scales and (2) their work is missing linguistic and psychological bipolarity tests which are recommended for better use of semantic di**ff**erential scales in user technology interactions (Verhagen, van den Hoo**ff**, and Meents 2015).**

**One consistent theme which can be observed across these body of works is that they lack the empirical rigor in development and validation that is noticeable in scale development studies geared towards measuring interpersonal trust (Lewis, Sycara, and Walker 2018; Söllner and Leimeister 2013). Apart from lacking empirical rigor, there have been no developments to build on these limitations which have been recognised in these works which has resulted in low uptake of such scales. Given this state of research, and the fact that it is important to be able to assess people’s trust in systems that are becoming increasingly intelligent and complex, we determined that it was necessary to conduct a study in order to provide a robust and empirically sound tool for assessing trust in user technology interactions.**

## 3. Model & hypothesis development

**As put forth earlier, the main aim of the current study is to test the attributes of a human computer trust model (HCTM) proposed initially by Sousa, Lamas, and Dias (2014) to ascertain if they capture the essence of and help measure trust. HCTM was developed in four phases comprising of an extensive literature review on trust, a word elicitation study to capture a rich set of its multi-disciplinary notions, participatory design sessions with users and uni**fi**cation of Davis (1989) and Venkatesh et al. (2003) technology acceptance models. As a result, Sousa, Lamas, and Dias (2014) were able to obtain a set of seven attributes (namely motivation, willingness, competence, benevolence, predictability, honesty and reciprocity) which would predict trust in user technology** **interactions. However, as with some of the models mentioned in the previous section, the major limitation with HCTM was that the attributes proposed in the model had not been empirically assessed to see if they actually do predict trust. To overcome this limitation, there have been two attempts within the literature to empirically assess its feasibility in user technology interactions. These are described as follows:**

**(1) The** fi**rst attempt was that of Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2017) who tested the model with the Estonian i-voting system. They found that certain attributes of the model namely competence, benevolence and honesty were signi**fi**cant while the other four attributes in the model did not have any** eff**ect on trust.**

**(2) Following the above study, Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018) further tested the model with Siri (Apple’s intelligent personal assistant). However, when testing the model, they retained all the statistically non-signi**fi**cant attributes from the previous study by Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2017). This was done based on the recommendations put forth by Hair Jr et al. (2016) who opine that when aim of the study is to contribute to scale development, non-signi**fi**cant attributes from initial studies cannot simply be discarded without testing them in di**ff**erent ways and in di**ff**erent contexts to ensure proper construct validity and reliability. Their study results further re**fi**ned the HCTM and they showed that four attributes, namely competence, benevolence, reciprocity and risk perception (which as we will explain in the next section was formed as a result of combining two lower-order constructs namely willingness and honesty) e**ff**ect trust in user technology interactions.**

**Despite their re**fi**nement of HCTM, Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018) put forth that more empirical testing is needed to ascertain which attributes of the model hold true before moving on to scale development. Therefore, for our study, we take into account this revised version of HCTM, and build on the work of Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018). The entire evolution of the model is depicted in Figure 1 and the current version of the model under investigation is represented in Figure 2. In the next section, we further explain the di**ff**erent attributes of HCTM.**

## 3.1. Perceived risk

**It is worth noting that when HCTM was initially proposed by Sousa, Lamas, and Dias (2014), there was no attribute particularly named as perceived risk. However,** **there were two attributes in their model namely honesty and willingness. Until the model was empirically assessed by Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018), the connection between these individual attributes was not explored. In their work, Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018) found that both honesty and willingness essentially measure a user’s risk perception when interacting with technical artefacts. They further recommended combining these two attributes into a higher-order construct ‘perceived risk’ and then empirically assess if it predicts user trust, a practice common in scale development studies (Hair Jr et al. 2016).**

**We de**fi**ne perceived risk as a subjective assessment on the part of the end user of the probability of a speci**fi**ed type of incident happening when using a technical artefact and how concerned they are with the consequences of their action. The notion of perceived risk particularly becomes important when interacting with AI systems which have a black box nature as earlier described. In such situations, it becomes hard for both the end user and the programmer to accurately predict how a system reaches a set of conclusions and whether or not the advice of such a system be trusted. This leads us to our** fi**rst hypothesis:**

H1. **There exists a statistically signi**fi**cant relationship between perceived risk associated with a technological interaction and user trust with that system.**

## 3.2. Benevolence

**In the interpersonal trust literature, benevolence has been understood as a trustee acting in the best interest of and always willing to extend help to the trustor (Mayer, Davis, and Schoorman 1995). Translating this to a technological context, it is understood as technology being able to provide adequate, e**ff**ective and responsive help to the end user which eventually helps the user attain speci**fi**c goals related to their interaction (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018; Benbasat and Wang 2005). Individuals who perceive that a technology can provide the needed help will perceive fewer risks and uncertainties associated with its use, which can eventually translate into higher trust and continual use of the technology (Mcknight et al. 2011). Consequently, we hypothesise:**

H2. **The greater the benevolence of a technological artefact, the higher the level of user trust associated with it.**

## 3.3. Competence

**Competence of system is a direct representation of whether or not it has all the features and the** **functionalities to perform its intended tasks (Mcknight et al. 2011). Essentially, if a user perceives technology to be competent (i.e. having all desired functionality to achieve a particular outcome), then there is a high likelihood that they would place trust and act on the advice and recommendations o**ff**ered by the technology (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018). This leads us to our third hypothesis:**

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 1. Evolution of HCTM (based on studies conducted by Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018).

H3. **The higher the competence associated with the use of a system, the greater the trust of the user with that system.**

## 3.4. Reciprocity

**The notion of reciprocity is based on a give and take relationship. It can be understood through the lens of the computers as social actors’ paradigm, according to** **which people mindlessly apply social rules and expec tations to computers, going so far as ascribing gender and personality to them (Nass, Steuer, and Tauber 1994). In their work, Nass, Steuer, and Tauber (1994) empirically demonstrated that when people feel helped by a computer, they reciprocate in kind by spending more time interacting with it. A similar assertion is also made by Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2017) who put forth: ‘if people feel computer has been helpful towards them, they respond in kind by deciding to adopt and continually use a system and develop a symbiotic relationship with that system’ (49). The general expectation is that users expect a reciprocal relationship from a system when interacting with it. They not only expect the system to respond to their needs but do so in a knowledgeable way. When the system does so, then the chance of a user trusting it are much higher. This leads us to our fourth hypothesis:**

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Figure 2. Research model under investigation.

H4. **There exists a positive relationship between reciprocity and trust in human technology interactions.**

## 4. Method

**We used a semi-structured questionnaire to validate HCTM using the concept of design** fi**ction (DF). DF** **has garnered great deal of interest in the HCI community recently, not just as a design approach but also as a research method (Schulte, Marshall, and Cox 2016; Derboven and Vandenberghe 2016). It has been de**fi**ned as the deliberate use of diegetic prototypes to suspend disbelief about change. To put it simply, DF allows envisioning how a future with current forms of technology might look like. It is not science** fi**ction wherein we purport something which does not exist yet. Instead, it takes into account the contemporary technical artefacts and allows us to imagine how interactions with them might look like in the future. It provides a method to probe, explore, and critique these possible futures and the technologies they embrace (Blythe 2014).**

**DF has been categorised into many types: speculative design, critical design, and future scenarios, to name a few (for a detailed overview, see Bleecker 2009). For the current study, we use the future scenarios approach. A future scenario has been described to be a common design method which makes it easy to communicate a future concept. It is either grounded in a present context or the very near future, and is developed with the ‘intentionality’ of implementation while being grounded in facts and limitations of current technology (Blythe 2014). It uses narratives or stories with the intention to communicate how such a technology would operate and therefore help elicit user perceptions about interacting with such technologies in the not so distant future. With the exponential increase in technological capabilities and complexities, and the ability of DF to be able to ask questions about potential implications (such as trust) of such technologies, we chose DF as a method to guide our study forward.**

## 4.1. Participants

**The data for the survey were collected through two independent studies using two futuristic scenarios (explained in detail in the next section), namely Homes for life (study 1) and New School (study 2). For study 1, a total of 118 valid responses were obtained, out of which 50 (42.37%) were female and 68 were male (57.63%). Most of the respondents were either between 18–27 years (44.07%) or 28–37 years (37.29%). Only 19 (16.10%) and 3 (2.54%) responses came from individuals between age groups 38–47 and 48–57, respectively. For the second study, a total of 183 valid responses were obtained, out of which 73 (39.9%) were females and 110 (60.1%) were males. A total of 101 (55.22%) responses came from people between 18 and 27 years of age, followed by 61 responses (33.3%) from individuals between 28 and 37 years. Only 14 (7.7%) and 7** **(3.8%) responses came from individuals between age groups 38–47 and 48–57, respectively.**

## 4.2. Materials & apparatus

**As put forth previously, we used two independent studies with two sets of future scenarios. The reasoning behind this is twofold. First, we wish to be empirically robust in our scale development process and second, we would like to compare results of both the studies to ascertain if attributes of HCTM which predict trust are consistent across both the studies and if not, then what can be done to further re**fi**ne the scale.**

**The** fi**rst scenario used for the study was ‘Homes for Life’. This scenario was developed by Schulte, Marshall, and Cox (2016) and is an interview-based story which is aimed at opening up the debate about the use of emergent ‘smart home’ technology, but at the same time touches upon privacy issues as well as parent-childrelationships. The second scenario which we used is called ‘New School’ which was developed by Derboven and Vandenberghe (2016) and is focused on a future where students’ learning activities are supervised by a tailor-made system. This scenario addresses the ethics of computer supervision/ support/surveillance, as well as the reliability of the data from such systems. In both the scenarios, issue of trust is of prime importance as the end users have to eventually be able to rely on and act upon the decision, advise and recommendations** off**ered by these systems. Therefore, these two scenarios were chosen to guide our scale development.**

**Regarding measures for the survey, since we were interested in building on the revised version of HCTM by Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018), we reworded the 14 items which were found signi**fi**cant in their study to measure participants’ perception of trust with future scenarios.**

## 4.3. Procedure

**We used a semi-structured questionnaire to collect data. The survey questionnaire was constructed in three languages- English, German and Estonian. Prior to distributing it, three researchers (who were native speakers of each of these languages) independently veri**fi**ed the accuracy of translations to ensure that there are no signi**fi**cant di**ff**erences between the original English items and the translated German and Estonian items. The next step involved piloting the survey with 3 information technology PhD students and 15 master level students enrolled in a human computer interaction course at a public university in Estonia to remove any poorly worded items. We enlisted help of public universities** **and professional organisations in Estonia to disseminate our research. Apart from this, snowball sampling was also used to amplify participation in the survey. Since both the scenarios used in the survey were lengthy to read (study 1 being 7 & study 2 being 6 pages in length), we also decided to convert entire text of the scenarios (borrowed from their respective research papers) into speech. We used a professional text-to-speech program called Natural Reader**<strong><sup>3</sup></strong> **which allows converting any written text into natural sounding voices. As a result, the audio version for study 1 was 21 min and 28 s and for study 2, it was 16 min and 9 s in length. At the beginning of each survey, participants were advised that they could choose to either read the scenario or listen to the audio. The data for the survey were collected from November 2018 to January 2019 and we used a 5-point likert scale where 1 indicates strongly disagree and 5 indicates strongly agree to collect participant responses.**

**To analyse the data obtained, we used partial least square structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). There are two main reasons behind doing so. First, our main goal through this research is theory development and not theory con**fi**rmation/testing, for which other covariance-based approaches such as con**fi**rmatory factor analysis are more appropriate (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017). Second, as has been put forth earlier, we are interested in re**fi**ning HCTM by identifying which are the key ‘driver-constructs’ that predict trust, and then gradually move towards scale development. Such an approach is predictive in nature as we are interested in identifying whether the exogenous (i.e. independent) constructs in HCTM are able to explain the endogenous (i.e. dependent) variable which is trust. Therefore, keeping in mind these study objectives and in line with the recommendations of Hair Jr et al. (2016), we chose PLS-SEM for the present study.**

## 5. Results

**The** fi**rst step in this stage includes specifying the PLS-SEM model. Within the trust literature, this step is often not made explicit which has led to measurement model misspeci**fi**cation, i.e. the model has been labelled as re**fl**ective when it should have been formative and vice versa (Söllner and Leimeister 2013). Consistent with prior research (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018; Mcknight et al. 2011), we model trust as a re**fl**ective endogenous construct based on the rationale that the indicators for the exogenous constructs will co-vary and are correlated to each other.**

**Before proceeding to the next steps, it is also important to ensure that the sample size meets the requirements for carrying out PLS-SEM. According to Hair Jr** **et al. (2016), the minimum sample size should be 10 times the maximum number of arrowheads pointing at a latent variable in a PLS path model. As can be observed from Figure 2, the maximum arrows which point to the latent variable of interest (trust) are 4. Therefore, in accordance with this recommendation, minimum sample size needed for PLS-SEM for our study is 40. We clearly exceed these requirements as both study 1 and study 2 had 118 & 183 participants, respectively. It should also be pointed out that all scales for analysing data in our study were positively worded, except perceived risk which was negatively worded and reversed prior to the analysis.**

## 5.1. Evaluation of the measurement model

**This step involves evaluating the reliability and validity of the construct measures to justify their inclusion in the path model. It includes reporting outer loadings, composite reliability (CR), Cronbach’s alpha (CA), average variance extracted (AVE), and discriminant validity (DV). We report these values for both studies as we are interested in comparing both results to ascertain which attributes of HCTM predict user trust. To reiterate, when we talk in terms of study 1 and study 2 in the following sections, we refer to ‘Homes for life’ and ‘New school’ scenarios, respectively, which were used to assess HCTM.**

**An initial analysis of the data revealed that outer load ings for REC01 (an indicator measuring reciprocity) was** −**0.060 in the** fi**rst and 0.648 in the second study (refer Tables 1 and 2). Both these values are less than 0.70 and as per the PLS-SEM guidelines, this indicator was dropped before proceeding to a full analysis (Hair Jr et al. 2016). As can be seen from Tables 1 and 2, convergent validity (assessed through reporting outer loadings and indicator reliability) and internal consistency reliability (assessed through reporting AVE, CR and CA) values are above their respective thresholds. This provides support for the measures’ reliability and validity. The** fi**nal step in measurement model evaluation is to check if DV is established. It is important as it helps assess if a construct is distinct from other constructs by empirical standards. As recommended by Hair Jr et al. (2016), we report the results from cross-loadings (CL) and Fornell–Larcker (FL) criterion.**

**With regards to CL values, DV is established when an indicators cross-loading on an assigned construct is higher than all of its cross-loadings with other constructs (Hair Jr et al. 2016). If we observe Tables 3 and 4, all highlighted values for every construct loads high only for that particular construct and not to any other construct. Moving on to analysing the FL values, a close** **observation of Tables 5 and 6 (logic being similar to that of analysing CL values), the values in bold along the diagonal are high for the construct which they are associated with across both row and column. This essentially means that all indicators of a corresponding construct load highly only for that particular construct and are ‘distinct’ from other indicators for other constructs. Thus, both CL and FL values taken together establish DV. Moreover, all the statistical tests thus far on the measurement model con**fi**rm valid and reliable construct measures and our instrument satis**fi**es requirement for internal consistency reliability, convergent and discriminant validity.**

## 5.2. Evaluation of the structural model

**This step involves examining the model’s predictive capabilities and the relationships between the constructs, i.e. to assess how well the exogenous constructs explain or predict the endogenous construct. First, we check the model for any collinearity issues by reporting the variance in**fl**ation factor (VIF) values. In study 1, the VIF values for benevolence, competence, perceived risk and** **reciprocity were 4.933, 4.802, 3.937 and 2.351 and in study 2, these were 2.724, 1.655, 1.933 and 2.027, respectively. In both cases, these were below the conservative threshold of 5 (Hair Jr et al. 2016), thereby indicating the absence of collinearity issues.**

**The next step is to test for statistical signi**fi**cance to ascertain which attributes of HCTM predict trust and should be included in the** fi**nal instrument. Consistent with the guidelines set forth by Hair Jr et al. (2016), we performed non-parametric bootstrapping with 5000 subsamples with 118 and 183 cases (sample sizes for study 1 and study 2, respectively) individually at a signi**fi**cance level of 0.05. As can be observed from Tables 7 and 8, for study 1, except H4 (Reciprocity**  **Trust) all other hypotheses are signi**fi**cant at a 0.05 level. For study 2, all hypotheses are statistically signi**fi**cant. Since the aim of the current study is to develop a robust psychometric scale for trust measurement, therefore we only wish to include those attributes which are statistically signi**fi**cant and accurately predict trust. However, as has been put forth by Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas (2018) and Hair Jr et al. (2016), reporting statistical signi**fi**cance is not** **enough to assess suitability of the model and has to be complemented by reporting other parameters such as** predictive relevance $( Q ^ { 2 } )$ and effect size $( f ^ { 2 }   )$ **.**

To report $Q ^ { 2 } ;$ **, we use a procedure called blindfolding, following a cross-validated redundancy approach. The** $Q ^ { 2 }$ **values for study 1 and study 2 are 0.627 and 0.498,** respectively. $Q ^ { 2 }$ **values larger than zero for a speci**fic **re**fl**ective endogenous variable (trust in this case) indicate the path models predictive relevance for that construct** (Hair Jr et al. 2016). Since both the $Q ^ { 2 }$ **values for study 1 and study 2 are above zero, we can state that the constructs which are statistically signi**fi**cant accurately pre-dict user trust. The next step is to report e**ffect size $( f ^ { 2 } )$ values which are an indicator of how each individual exogenous construct contributes to the endogenous construct. For study 1, $, f ^ { 2 }$ values for benevolence, competence and perceived risk are 0.107, 0.174 and 0.165, respectively. Similarly, for study 2, the $f ^ { 2 }$ values for benevolence, competence and perceived risk are 0.075, 0.086 and 0.115, respectively. These values will always vary depending on the context and can also change each time for the same context (Hair Jr et al. 2016). For **instance, in the case for homes for life scenario (study 1), competence had the most a**ff**ect on trust followed by perceived risk and benevolence whereas in the case** **for new school (study 2), perceived risk has the highest** aff**ect on user trust followed by competence and benevolence.**

**The** fi**nal step in the assessment of the structural model is reporting coe**fficient of determination $( R ^ { 2 } )$ values. This represents exogenous latent variables’ combined effect on the endogenous latent variable and it is interpreted in the same way as in a conventional regression analysis procedure (Hair Jr et al. 2016). In study $1 ,   R ^ { 2 }$ and $R ^ { 2 }$ **adjusted values are 0.834 and 0.828,** respectively, whereas in study 2, $R ^ { 2 }$ and $R ^ { 2 }$ **adjusted values are 0.699 and 0.692, respectively. According to** Hair Jr et al. (2016), $R ^ { 2 }$ **values of 0.75, 0.50 or 0.25 are considered substantial, moderate or weak. In line with** this, for study 1, both $R ^ { 2 }$ and $R ^ { 2 }$ **adjusted are substantial whereas in study 2, these are moderate (but close to being substantial). More speci**fi**cally, we can say that in study 1, around 83% of changes in technology trust can be explained by the statistically signi**fi**cant exogenous variables in HCTM while in study** $2 ,$ **around 69% of changes in trust are explained by these variables. In both cases, the statistically signi**fi**cant attributes signi**fi**cantly predict user trust in human technology interactions.**

**Keeping in mind all the empirical values obtained thus far, it is safe to say that our model passes the criteria for both the measurement and structural model evalu ation, and the** fi**nal scale exhibits good validity, reliability and predictive power.**

## 6. Discussions

**The objective of the current study was to build on prior works (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018) and empirically assess HCTM to ascertain which attributes of the model hold true in user-technology interactions. We used the concept of future scenarios and assessed** **user perception of trust across two scenarios namely ‘Homes for life’ and ‘New School’. Our study results found three attributes namely benevolence, competence and perceived risk to be statistically signi**fi**cant. The** fi**nal version of the human computer trust scale (HCTS), obtained as a result of re**fi**ning HCTM is pre-sented in Appendix 1 and consists of 12 items. Our research contributions are twofold. First, by acknowledging limitations of past work (refer Section 2.1) on measuring trust, we addressed the fact that these works lack the empirical rigor which is noticeable in scale development studies geared towards measuring interpersonal trust and present a rigorous and a systematic study on scale development to measure trust in user technology interactions. Second, to the best of our knowledge, this is one of the** fi**rst studies to use the concept of future scenarios to model trust. We built on the work of Schulte, Marshall, and Cox (2016) who opined that design** fi**ction and future scenarios can be used as a research method and encourage future studies to use this approach to measure other facets of user interactions (e.g. assessing user experience, anxiety, etc.) in HCI.**

## 6.1. Study limitations

**Our study is not without its limitations which can serve as directions for future research. First, prior research has shown that culture has an in**fl**uence on trust in user technology interactions (Vance, Elie-Dit-Cosaque, and Straub 2008). Future research can take this into account and test how well the HCTS fares across di**ff**erent cultures and contexts. Prior research has also demonstrated that trust is a dynamic construct and it evolves over time. It can either be lost or rebuilt due to context and/or reassessment of behaviours and intention on the part of the end user (Mcknight et al. 2011). This can also be** **addressed in future research which can take the form of longitudinal studies which can use HCTS to see if it is able to capture these user trust dynamics. Finally, future research can look into ways as to how the current scale can be operationalised so that it can be useful to technologists and practitioners.**

## Appendices

## Appendix 1. Final Scale

**After working on empirically re**fi**ning HCTM based on prior works (Gulati, Sousa, and Lamas 2017, 2018), the re**fi**ned version of HCTM now consists of the following 12 items:**

**(1) I believe that there could be negative consequences when using (—)**

**(2) I feel I must be cautious when using (—)**

**(3) It is risky to interact with (—)**

**(4) I believe that (—) will act in my best interest**

**(5) I believe that (—) will do its best to help me if I need help**

**(6) I believe that (—) is interested in understanding my needs and preferences**

**(7) I think that (—) is competent and e**ff**ective in (—)**

**(8) I think that (—) performs its role as (—) very well** **(9) I believe that (—) has all the functionalities I would expect from (—)**

**(10) If I use (—), I think i would be able to depend on it completely**

**(11) I can always rely on (—) for (—)**

**(12) I can trust the information presented to me by (—)**

**Since our purpose of developing the scale is that HCI researchers can use this in their research, therefore, to make it easy and less time consuming, we present our scale using placeholders [we refer to the brackets with dashes as presented above (—) as a placeholder]. This placeholder needs to be** fi**lled in by the user of the scale. We illustrate this as follows:**

**For instance, in item 1,2,3,4,5,6, 10 & 12, the placeholder needs to be replaced with the artefact with which the user of the scale intends to measure trust. For instance, if the artefact is Amazon ‘Alexa’, then the placeholder can simply be replaced by ‘Alexa’. In item 7, 8, 9 & 11, the initial placeholder needs to be replaced by the artefact (just like the previous items). However, the second placeholder needs to be replaced with the functionality of the artefact or what the artefact is capable of doing.**

**Again, if we use Alexa as an example, then for item 7, the** fi**rst placeholder would be replaced by ‘Alexa’ and the second placeholder can be replaced with any functionality of Alexa which the user of the scale wants to use to gauge trust perception. As an example, for item 7, second placeholder could be replaced by ‘providing personal assistance’. So, the** fi**nal sentence for item 7 using Alexa as an example would look like ‘I think that Alexa is competent and e**ff**ective in providing personal assistance’. To iterate, it doesn’t have to be ‘providing personal assistance’. What goes in the placeholder depends on the context, study objectives and the motives of the researcher. Essentially, the placeholders are there for putting the name of the artefact and their context of use.**
